chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, raising it, from Abdullah ibn Muskan who said:

We were a group of our companions, and we entered the bathhouse. So when we went out, we met Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), so he said to us: ‘Where are you coming back from?’ So we said to him, ‘From the bathhouse’. So he said: ‘May Allah purify your bathing’. So we said to him, ‘May we be sacrificed for you’. And we went with him until he entered the bathhouse. So we sat around (waiting) for him until he came out. So we said to him, ‘May Allah purify your bathing’. So he said: ‘May Allah clean you all’.

key_terms.جُعِلْنَا فِدَاكَ: May we be sacrificed for you (a common expression of devotion)

ai.seo_question: What is the etiquette and supplication associated with visiting the bathhouse in Shia tradition?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the Imam’s attentiveness to the daily routines of his companions, transforming a mundane visit to the bathhouse into an opportunity for spiritual blessing (*barakah*). The reciprocal exchange of supplications highlights the Shia emphasis on mutual spiritual support and the sanctification of physical cleanliness (*taharah*) as a precursor to spiritual purity. It underscores the Imam’s role not just as a religious authority, but as a compassionate guide who sanctifies the ordinary aspects of his followers' lives.

en.sarwar: Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Ali ibn al-Hassan al-Taymiy from Muhammad ibn abu Hamzah from ‘Umar ibn Yazid who has said the following: “Abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has said that ’Amir al-Mu’minin has said, ‘You must not lie down on your back in the bathhouse; it melts the fat of kidneys and must not rub your feet with pottery because it may cause leprosy.”’
